Their disagreement is this: the worshippers believe in one God while the polytheists oppose them and curse them, whereas the polytheists hope for their intercession and their bringing them near to Allah in nearness.

It has been said: when the Muslims asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", they acknowledged and said, "Allah." Then when they asked them, "Why do you worship idols?", they said, "We worship them only so that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness." So the pronoun in ﴿between them﴾ refers to them and to the Muslims. The meaning is: Allah will judge on the Day of Resurrection between the disputing parties of both groups.

The meaning of the denial of guidance is: withholding of divine kindness (lutf), as a mark against them, indicating that no kindness is granted to them, and that they are, in Allah's knowledge, among the doomed. [Mahmud said: "The meaning of the denial of guidance is the withholding of kindness, as a mark against them, indicating that kindness will not be shown to them, and that they are, in His knowledge, among the doomed." Ahmad said: The doctrine of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) is to take this verse and its like at face value. Their belief is that the meaning of Allah's guidance of the believer is His creating guidance in him, and the meaning of His misguiding the disbeliever is removing him from guidance and creating disbelief in him. Nonetheless, according to the People of the Sunnah, it is permissible that Allah creates for the disbeliever a kindness by which he would believe willingly, against the view of the Qadariyyah (the Determinists of the Free-Will school). Our purpose is to draw attention to the doctrine of the people of truth, and nothing else.]

It is read: ﴿kadhdhab﴾ and ﴿kadhub﴾ [both intensive forms of "liar"].

Their lie is their saying, concerning some of those whom they took as allies besides Allah, that they are "daughters of Allah." For this reason He follows it, arguing against them with His saying, ﴿If Allah had wished to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾. The meaning: if He wished to take a son, it would have been impossible and invalid, because it is inconceivable, and it could only occur by His choosing some of His creation, singling them out and bringing them near, as a man singles out his son and brings him close. He has done this with the angels, and you were deceived by it and his singling them out misled you, so you claimed they were His children, through your ignorance of Him and of His reality, which differs from the realities of bodies and accidents. As if He said: if He wished to take a son, He would not exceed what He did by choosing whom He willed from His creation, namely the angels; but because of your ignorance you supposed that choosing them meant taking them as children. Then you persisted in your ignorance and folly, and made them daughters, so you were liars, disbelievers, extravagant in fabrication against Allah and His angels, excessive in disbelief. [His saying "extravagant in fabrication" is perhaps: "exaggerating" (mubalighin). (ʿ)] [His saying "excessive in disbelief" is perhaps: "exaggerating" (ghalin). (ʿ)]

Then He said, ﴿Glorified is He﴾, exalting His essence above having any of what they attributed to Him of children or allies. He indicated this by what contradicts it, which is that He is One, so it is not possible for Him to have a consort, for if He had a consort, she would be of His kind, and He has no kind. When it is not possible for Him to have a consort, it is not possible for Him to have a son. This is the meaning of His saying, ﴿How could He have a son when He has no consort?﴾

He is the Subduer, the Overpowering over everything, and among things are their gods; so He overpowers them. How then could they be His allies and partners?

Then He indicated, through the creation of the heavens and the earth, the winding of each of the two (night and day) around the other, the subjugation of the two luminaries (the sun and the moon) and their running for a specified term, the dispersal of humankind in their great numbers from a single soul, and the creation of the livestock, that He is One, without partner, the Subduer who cannot be overcome.

Al-takwir (winding, wrapping) means folding and coiling. It is said: "he wound the turban on his head and wrapped it (kawwaraha)." It has several interpretations. Among them: night and day alternate, one going and the other covering its place. When one covers the place of the other, it is as if it has dressed it and wrapped around it, as clothing is wrapped around the one who wears it. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma describing the mirage:

*Its borders wind around its passes, folded like the folds of a robe over the gates of the narrow tracks.*
*And a still pool of the sun, bitter-hot, against which the swords of the people were raised, with spears of the Mahri breed, slender-bent.*

*When the two heights of an unknown wasteland contend, it casts forth the edges of its rain, woven like silk brocade.*

*Its borders wind around its passes, folded like the folds of a robe over the gates of the narrow tracks.*

*As if it, and the ruha, were death pursuing it, its manes are the crest of a white one beneath the wind, carried along.*

He is describing the mirage. "Still pool of the sun" refers to what falls from it onto the ground. Al-ajaj is an intensive form, meaning one of great blazing; it is said: "the fire blazed (ajjat al-nar ajijan): it flared up," and "the heat intensified." And "al-zalim (the male ostrich) rushed (ajja ajjan): it sped and made a rustling sound." And "the matter became confused (ajja al-amr)." Al-ajj is a white bird, swift in flight, resembling the ostrich. The mirage, at the intensity of heat, appears white as if it is moving; so it is permissible that the word is derived from the first (the swift bird), and it is permissible that it is attributed to the latter, since it resembles it. The lam is for the specification of time, and al-qawadib are the cutting swords.

Al-Mahriyya: the horses ascribed to Mahr ibn Haydan, the ancestor of a tribe of Yemen, whose horses are the noblest horses. Al-awaj is the plural of awjaʼ, also a fine type of them. Al-halan are the elevation and depression of the land. Al-majhal is a place unknown to the traveller. Al-qadhf (on the pattern of sabab) is that which casts out what is in it, so no one is in it. Al-mutarrad is the level mirage, likened to brocade woven in its evenness and whiteness. Al-thanaya are the steep passes. Al-haqw is the waist and the waistband, and tightening it on him is a metaphor for the side of the pass. The borders of the mirage (hawashi al-sarab) are its sides. Al-mala' (with a damma and a long vowel) is the collective noun of mala'a, which is the outer cloak. Al-tafarij is a small gate and a garment of silk brocade. Al-rahwa (plural of rahw) are elevated places, and the term is also applied to low ground. It is also said to be the name of a place. Al-mawt is the desert wasteland. Al-rakd is striking the animal with the foot, and striking in general; here it is a figurative usage in the manner of tasrihiyya (a metaphor in which the borrowed term is the verb). Al-a'raf is the plural of ʻarf. The ʻarf of the rooster and of the horse is the uppermost hair of the neck. And a'raf al-bahr and al-sayl means when its waves pile up and rise like crests. Al-azhar: the white cloud and white water, and this is most fitting with its being "beneath the wind," because the apparent meaning of the first contradicts His saying ﴿it carries heavy clouds﴾. Al-mantuj is that which the wind brings forth and drives until it drips.

He says: many a still pool of the sun, meaning the mirage of extreme heat or movement, the swords of my people were raised against it in the moment, along with noble horses, when the low and high parts of the barren land pull against each other, the edges of the mirage. He likened the encirclement of its sides and its piling up along the sides of the pass to the folding of a cloak over the gates of narrow tracks. "Tala" (wind around): it may be the answer of "dha" (when), and it may be an attribute of "mutarrad," and its answer is what precedes it, indicating it. The folding is ascribed to the passes because they are the cause of the twisting. "Laww al-mala'" is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). "A'raf" is the predicate of "ka'anna." "Al-Rahwa" is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya). The subject of "yarkud" is either the pronoun of the mirage or the pronoun of the rahwa, since they seem to strike one another. It is also related: "tatrudu" (it drives it away), and its subject is definitely the pronoun of the rahwa, because the mirage is the one driven away.

The line in the Kashshaf reads: "yalwi al-thanaya bi-ahqiha." Al-haqw, its plural is ahaqq, and its original pattern is af'al.

Another interpretation: each of them covers the other when it arrives upon it, so in its covering of it, it is likened to a visible thing folded over what hides it from the sights of the eyes. Another: this one rolls over that one in successive rolling, so that is likened to the successive layers of a turban, one upon the trace of another.

﴿Behold, He is the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾ — the Mighty, the Overpowering, Able to punish those who persist (in sin), the Forgiving to the sins of those who repent.

[[Mahmud said: "that is, to the sins of those who repent." Ahmad said: The truth is that He is Forgiving to those who repent and to whomever He wills among those who persist in what is less than shirk, and (He is forgiving to) those who despair of Allah's mercy. Al-Zamakhshari has restricted the verse to what you see.]]

Or, "the Mighty" is the Overpowering who is able to hasten the punishment upon them, yet He forbears toward them and delays them until a specified term; so He named His forbearance toward them "forgiveness."

If you say: what is the sense of His words ﴿then He made from it its mate﴾, and what does "then" (thumma) imply of delay (tarakhi)? I answer: these are two signs. [[Mahmud said: "If you say: what is the sense of the conjunction with thumma in His words ﴿then He made﴾, I answer that they are two signs... etc." Ahmad said: What prevented him from taking thumma to indicate delay in existence is that it falls between the creation of the offspring from Adam and the creation of Eve from him, and she is prior to the offspring, let alone being delayed relative to their creation. So it cannot be taken as delay in existence, since in the other interpretation he links it to a single meaning, on the assumption: ﴿He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate﴾, meaning: He paired her with her mate. Thus here it retains its original sense of delay in existence. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best.]] Among the signs that he enumerated as indicating His oneness and power is the splitting of this vast creation from the single soul of Adam and the creation of Hawwa (Eve) from his short rib. However, the one was made by God a continuous customary practice, while the other was not subject to custom; no female other than Eve was created from a man's short rib. So it is more fitting as a sign and more striking to the wonder of the hearer. He therefore joined it with thumma to the first sign, to indicate its distinction from it in excellence and distinction, and its delay from it with respect to the increase in its being a sign. So this is delay in status and rank, not delay in existence. It has also been said: thumma is connected to a single meaning, as if it were said: He created you from a single soul, then God paired it with a mate. It has also been said: He brought forth the offspring of Adam from his back like particles, then after that created Hawwa. ﴿And He sent down for you﴾: He decreed for you and apportioned for you, because His decrees and apportionments are described as descending [[Mahmud said: "He only made it descending because His decrees and apportionments are described as descending..." etc. Ahmad said: From this very same pattern is the saying of the rajiz:

Humps of camels in a cloud.]] from the sky, where He wrote on the Preserved Tablet: every existent that will exist. It has also been said: livestock cannot live except by vegetation, vegetation cannot subsist except by water, and He has sent down water, so it is as if He sent them down. It has also been said: He created them in Paradise and then sent them down. ﴿Eight pairs﴾: male and female, from the camels, the cattle, the sheep and the goats. A "zawj" (pair) is the name for one that has another with it; when it stands alone it is an odd number (fard) and an unpaired one (watr). God the Exalted said: ﴿so He made of it the two mates, the male and the female﴾. ﴿Creation after creation﴾: a living, complete being; after bones clothed with flesh; after bare bones; after a lump of flesh; after a clot; after a drop. And the "three darknesses" are: the belly, the womb and the placenta. It has also been said: the loins, the womb and the belly. ﴿That is God, your Lord, to whom belong the kingdom; there is no god but He; so how are you turned away?﴾ Him whose acts are these, how could you be diverted from His worship to the worship of another?

Indeed, Allah is free of need of you [of your faith], and you are the ones who need Him, because you harm yourselves by disbelief and benefit yourselves by faith. ﴿And He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾, out of mercy toward them, because it casts them into ruin. ﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾, meaning He approves gratitude for you, because it is the cause of your success and well-being. Therefore He did not dislike your disbelief, nor did He approve your gratitude, except for your own sake and for your good. [[Al-Zamakhshari took *al-ridā* (approval) to mean *al-irāda* (will), and "His servants" to mean all people in general... etc.]] It is not because a benefit returns to Him, since He is the Self-Sufficient, to whom need cannot apply. Some deviants have indeed strained to establish for Allah, exalted is He, that He does not approve for His servants disbelief, which He has negated of Himself, and said: "This is a general statement intended in a specific sense, and He meant only His servants whom He referred to in His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾," meaning the protected ones (*al-ma'ṣūmīn*), like His saying: ﴿A spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾. Exalted is Allah above what the wrongdoers say. [[His saying "to establish for Allah … etc." holds only if *al-riḍā* means *al-irāda*, which is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. According to the People of the Sunnah, it is other than will: the disbelief of the disbeliever is willed but not approved. According to the Mu'tazilah, it is neither willed nor approved. (ʿ)]]

It was read as *yarḍahu* with a *ḍamma* on the *hā'* whether connected or not, and with it sukūn (*yarḍah*). *Khawwalahu* means "he gave him." Abu al-Najm said:

*All praise belongs to Allah, the Giver, the Bestower,*
*Who gave and did not withhold, and was not made miserly toward.*
*Camels with humped backs, from the bounty of the one who bestows.*

*Al-wahhūb*: the Bestower. *Al-mujzil*: the one who gives abundantly; he explained it with his saying, "He gave to the askers and did not withhold from them." *Wa lam yubakhkhal* (with the *bā'* doubled, in the passive voice): meaning he was not accused of miserliness. It was also said that it is emphatic. It is related with the verb built in the active voice, meaning he did not make those he gave to into misers, but made them generous. *Kawma al-dhurā*: an accusative object of *a'ṭā*, meaning she-camels of great humps. *Al-kawm* is the plural of *kawmā'*. *Al-dhurā* is the plural of *dhirwah*. *Al-mukhawwal* with the doubled *wāw* is the giver, and that is Allah, mighty and majestic.

As for its real meaning, there are two possibilities. The first: that it means making Him a keeper of wealth, from the saying "he is a *khā'il* of wealth" or "*khāl* of wealth," when one is attentive to it and manages it well. From this is what is reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): that he would take care of his companions with admonition. [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, and more complete than it.]] The second: that it means He makes it *yakhwalu*, from *khāla yakhūlu*, when he was proud and boasted. Its meaning is found in the saying of the Arabs:

*Indeed, the wealthy man has a long train, swaggering.*

What he used to call upon [God] for: that is, he forgot the harm which he used to call upon God to remove. It is also said: he forgot his Lord, to whom he used to humble himself and supplicate earnestly, and "mā" here means "man" (the one who), like the statement of God Most High: ﴿وَما خَلَقَ الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنْثى﴾ (By Him Who created the male and the female).

It was read as "li-yuḍilla" (so that he may lead astray) with a fatḥah and with a ḍammah on the bā' (the vowel on the letter bā'), meaning that the result of his making rivals to God is his straying from the way of God, or his leading others astray.

A result may be the aim of an action, and it may be something other than the aim. His saying ﴿تَمَتَّعْ بِكُفْرِكَ﴾ (Enjoy your disbelief for a while) belongs to the category of khudhlān (abandonment, leaving someone to his own devices) and takhliyah (leaving him alone). It is as if He said to him: since you have refused to accept what you were commanded regarding faith and obedience, it is your right that you not be commanded to it after this, and that you be commanded to abandon it, as an intensification of His abandoning him and leaving him to his own affairs. There is no intensification of abandonment beyond this, since nothing is more severe than that he be driven to the opposite of what he was commanded. Its counterpart in meaning is His saying ﴿مَتاعٌ قَلِيلٌ ثُمَّ مَأْواهُمْ جَهَنَّمُ﴾ (A brief enjoyment, then their refuge is Hell).

Read with the light (short) vowel on the initial hamza, the word أمن becomes the interrogative hamza placed before مَن. Read with the emphatic (doubled) consonant, it becomes أم with مَن after it. مَن is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, the full sense being: "Is the one who is devotedly obedient (qanit) like the one who is not?" It was omitted because the context indicates it, since the disbeliever was mentioned just before. What follows, ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾, supports this. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Is the one who is devotedly obedient better, or the one who is a disbeliever?" Or it may be read as a continuous interrogative: "Is this one better, or the one who is devotedly obedient?"

Qanit means one who performs what is obligatory upon him of obedience. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best prayer is the one with the longest qunut" [[Narrated by Muslim through the route of Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir. al-Tahawi narrated it through this route with the wording "the longest standing" (tul al-qiyam), and it is likewise in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Ja'far with the wording: "He was asked, which prayer is best? He said: the longest standing."]], which means standing in it. From this is the qunut in the witr prayer, because it is the supplication of the one praying while standing, prostrating (sajidan) as a circumstance.

It was also read: ساجد وقائم (sajid wa qa'im), taking them as a predicate following a predicate, with the conjunction "and" joining the two attributes.

It was also read: ﴿and fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾.

By "those who know" he meant those who act upon their knowledge among the scholars of the religion, as if he regarded whoever does not act as not knowing. In this there is a great disparagement of those who acquire the sciences and then do not act upon them, and are then tested by the world, so they are, in the sight of God, ignorant, since He made the devoutly obedient ones the scholars. It may also be taken as a comparison, meaning: just as those who know and those who do not know are not equal, so too are the devoutly obedient and the disobedient not equal.

It has been said that it was revealed concerning Ammar ibn Yasir (may Allah be pleased with him) and Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi.

On the authority of al-Hasan: he was asked about a man who persists in sins and hopes [for God's mercy]. He said: "This is wishful thinking (tamanni); hope is only His words: ﴿...﴾." And he recited this verse. [[Mahmud said: "al-Hasan was asked about one who persists in sins and hopes... etc." Ahmad said: The statement of al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) is sound, but it does not apply to the statement of al-Zamakhshari given the context of his situation. For al-Hasan meant that the one who persists in sin, obstinate in it and not repentant, if his hope overcomes his fear, is then wishful; because what befits such a person is that his fear overcomes his hope. al-Hasan did not intend to despair this person of the mercy of God Most High, far be it. As for the context of al-Zamakhshari's situation, it is completed upon what he concealed of presenting this statement, for his belief is that such a disobedient person, even if he is a monotheist, must be eternal in the Fire of Hell, and there is no sense in his hoping. To strengthen the soundness of this belief he presented the statement of al-Hasan as a commitment to completing this tendency, and before long his hearing will be struck by what is in the reports of this surah.]]

It was also read: إنما يذّكر (innama yadhdhakkaru) with idgham (assimilation of the ta' into the dhal).

In this world: it is connected to "do good" (aḥsanū), not to "good" (ḥasanah). The meaning is: those who did good in this world, for them is a good (ḥasanah) in the Hereafter. This is entry into Paradise, that is, a good that cannot be described. Al-Suddī connected it to ḥasanah and interpreted the ḥasanah as good health and well-being.

If you say: when the adverbial phrase is connected to aḥsanū, its grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) is clear, so what is the meaning of connecting it to ḥasanah? It cannot be a qualifier of it, since it precedes it. I answer: it is a qualifier of it when it follows, and when it precedes it is an explanation of its place. So the preceding position does not prevent the connection, even though the connection is not a qualification in form or meaning.

"God's earth is spacious" means that there is no excuse at all for those who fall short in doing good, even if they plead their homelands and countries, and that they cannot devote themselves there to doing good and directing their resolve towards it. It is said to them: God's earth is spacious and His lands are many, so do not remain in helplessness, but move to other lands, and follow the prophets and the righteous in their emigration to other than their lands, so that they may increase their good deeds upon their good deeds and their obedience upon their obedience.

It is also said: this refers to those who were in the land of the polytheists and were commanded to emigrate from it, as in His saying: "Was not God's earth spacious, so that you might emigrate therein?" It is also said: it refers to the land of Paradise.

"Those who are patient" are those who endured separation from their homelands and kinsfolk, and other things, from swallowing bitter draughts and bearing trials in obedience to God and in increasing good. "Without reckoning" means they will not be called to account for it. It is also said: without measure and without balance, they will be given it in handfuls, and this is a figure of speech for abundance. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: it cannot be reached by reckoning, and its amount is not known.

It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "On the Day of Resurrection God will set up the scales. The people of prayer will be brought and their rewards will be paid out by the scales. The people of charity will be brought and their rewards will be paid out by the scales. The people of pilgrimage will be brought and their rewards will be paid out by the scales. The people of affliction will be brought, and no scale will be set up for them and no register will be spread out for them, and reward will be poured upon them in a flood." God the Exalted said: "Only those who are patient will be given their reward without reckoning," until the people of well-being in this world wish that their bodies had been cut with scissors, because of the excellence that the people of affliction receive.

[It was narrated by al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn Mardawayh, from the hadith of Anas, may God be pleased with him. Its chain is very weak. Abū Nuʿaym cited it in al-Ḥilya in the biography of Jābir ibn Zayd, from al-Ṭabarānī. It is in his Muʿjam with its chain going to Qatādah, from Jābir ibn Zayd, from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, in abbreviated form.]

Say: "Indeed I have been commanded to worship God, making religion sincerely His," and "I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims" (ﷺ)... 

Wait, I must translate faithfully. Here is the translation:

Say, "Indeed I have been commanded to devote the religion sincerely to Him, and I have been commanded to that for the sake of being the first of the Muslims," meaning their leader and foremost in this world and the Hereafter. And the meaning is that sincerity (ikhlas) has precedence in religion, so whoever is sincere is foremost. If you ask: how is "umirtu" conjoined to "umirtu" when they are one? [[Mahmud said: "If you ask: how is 'umirtu' conjoined to 'umirtu' when they are one? He answered that it is not a repetition..." etc. Ahmad said: He excelled in strengthening this meaning in this verse with His words "so worship what you will besides Him" (39:15), for its contrast with non-restriction necessitates that it be restrictive, and God knows best. And how excellent is what he has explained of the aspects of hyperbole in describing God's glorification of the enormity of their loss, when he said:

He began the sentence and opened it with the particle of alerting (ala), placed a separation between the subject and the predicate, defined "the loss" and described it as "manifest." He also mentioned in naming Satan "taghut" three aspects of hyperbole: first, naming him with the verbal noun, as if he were the very essence of transgression; second, forming it on the pattern fa'lut, which is an intensive form like rahmut (vast mercy) and malakut (dominion) and the like; third, placing its lam before its ayn to indicate that Satan is specifically singled out by this name.]] I say: they are not one, because their two aspects differ. The command to sincerity and its imposition is one thing, and the command to it in order that its performer may secure the prize of precedence in religion is another. When the two aspects and attributes of a thing differ, it is treated as two different things. You may also make the lam extra (ziyada), like it in "aradtu li-an af'al" (I wished to do), and it is only added with "an" specifically, not with an explicit noun, as if it were added as a substitute for abandoning the original to what stands in its place, just as the sin was added in "istaṭā'a" as a substitute for abandoning the original which is "uṭīʿa." The evidence for this aspect is its coming without the lam in His words: "And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims" and "I have been commanded that I be among the believers," and "I have been commanded that I be the first to submit." In its meaning there are several aspects: that I be the first to submit in my era and among my people, since he was the first to oppose the religion of his fathers and to cast off and smash the idols; and that I be the first of those I call to Islam to submit; and that I be the first to call himself to what he calls others to, so that I may be an example in my speech and action altogether, and that my attribute not be the attribute of kings who command what they do not do; and that I do the deeds of the foremost that entitle me to precedence, as an indication of cause by effect, meaning: God has commanded me to make religion sincerely His, free of polytheism, ostentation, and every impurity, by the evidence of reason and revelation.

If I disobey my Lord by opposing the two proofs, I deserve His punishment, so I will not disobey Him nor follow your command, and that is when they called him to the religion of his fathers. If you ask: what is the meaning of the repetition in His words "Say, I have been commanded to worship God, making religion sincerely His," and His words "Say, God I worship, making my religion sincerely His"? I say: it is not a repetition, because the first is information that he is commanded by God to initiate worship and sincerity, and the second is information that he singles out God alone, to the exclusion of others, in worshipping Him, making religion sincerely His. To indicate this, he placed the object of worship before the act of worship in the second and postponed it in the first; the first sentence concerns the act itself and its bringing into being, and the second concerns the one for whose sake the act is performed. For this reason His words "so worship what you will besides Him" are arranged upon it. The purpose of this command, which comes in the form of choice, is hyperbole in abandonment and leaving to oneself, as I have verified in discussing it twice. Say: the complete in loss, gathering its aspects and causes, are those "who have lost themselves" by falling into a destruction after which there is no destruction, "and their families" — for if they were among the people of the Fire, they have lost them as they lost themselves, and if they were among the people of Paradise, they have gone from them in a departure with no return to them. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verse 16:

﴿And beneath them will be layers of Fire, and above them layers [of Fire].﴾ The meaning of "from beneath them" is "layers of Fire," and "they are canopies for others." That punishment is what Allah threatens His servants with, to frighten them, so that they avoid what would bring them into it. ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾: do not expose yourselves to what would incur My wrath. This is an admonition from Allah, Exalted is He, and a far-reaching counsel. It has been read: "Yā ʿibādī" (O My servants).

Al-Tāghūt is a form from ṭughyān (transgression), like al-malakūt and al-raḥamūt, except that in it there is a metathesis (qalb), placing the lām before the ʿayn. It has been applied to Satan or to the devils, since it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and in it there are intensive forms (mubālaghāt): the naming by the verbal noun, as if the very essence of Satan were transgression, and that the pattern is an intensive pattern, for al-raḥamūt means vast mercy, and al-malakūt means extensive dominion. The metathesis is for specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), since it is not applied to anything other than Satan. The intended meaning here is the plural. It is also read al-ṭawāghīt. An-yaʿbudūhā is a substitute (badal) for al-ṭāghūt, a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl). Lahumu al-bushrā is the good news of reward, like the verse: ﴿They shall have good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾.

God, exalted is He, gives them good news of this in His revelation through the tongues of His messengers, and the angels meet them at the arrival of death bearing good news, and when they are gathered. God the Exalted said: ﴿On the day you see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and on their right hands: "Good news for you today: gardens..."﴾

By His servants who listen to the word and follow the best of it, He means those who avoid and turn in repentance, and no others. He intended that they be upon this description together with avoidance and repentance, so the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun. He intended that they be critics in religion, distinguishing between the good and the better, and the excellent and the more excellent; so when two matters confront them, obligatory and recommended, they choose the obligatory, and likewise the permissible and the recommended, eager for what is nearer to God and greater in reward. Under this falls the schools of thought, and choosing the most firmly established of them upon examination and the strongest upon testing, and the clearest in evidence or indication, and that you not be in a school merely by imitation, as the poet said:

*Gird up your resolve in the matters of religion, and strive; and do not be like a donkey led on a halter, obediently following.*

[Al-Zamakhsharī's words: "Gathering up the garments from the forearm" is a metaphor for abandoning laziness. Then he said: strive in the rulings of religion and do not follow others blindly, lest you be like a donkey that a man leads and it follows, obeying him wherever he directs it. It may also mean: strive in action and do not obey Satan.]

He means the blind follower (muqallid). It was also said: they listen to the Qur'an and other things and follow the Qur'an. It was said: they listen to the commands of God and follow the best of them, such as retaliation and pardon, vindication and forbearance, and open and private giving, in accordance with His words: ﴿But that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ and ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾. From Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: he is the man who sits with a people, hears a discourse containing both good points and faults, and relates the best of what he heard and refrains from the rest.

Among the pauses (waqf): some stop at ﴿So give good news to My servants﴾ and begin with ﴿Those who listen﴾, reading it as nominative by way of beginning, its predicate being ﴿those are...﴾.

The original sense of the speech: "Is then one against whom the word of punishment has become due [to be rescued]? Then are you to rescue him?" It is a conditional clause into which the interrogative of denial (hamzat al-inkar) and the fa' (the particle of consequence, fa' al-jaza') entered. Then the fa' that stood at its beginning entered for conjunction (li-l-'atf) upon an elided element indicated by the address, its estimate being:

"Are you the master of their affair? Then whoever has the punishment due upon him, you rescue him?" The second hamza is the first, repeated to emphasize the meaning of denial and improbability. The phrase man fi al-nar ("those in the Fire") is placed in the position of the pronoun. Thus, according to this view, the verse is one single sentence.

Another possibility: the verse is two sentences: "Then is one against whom the punishment has become due [...], are you then going to free him? Are you then going to rescue those in the Fire?" The elision of "fa-anta tukhlisuhu" ("are you then going to free him") is permissible because "a-fa-anta tunqidhu" ("are you then going to rescue") indicates it. Their being deserving of punishment while in this world is treated as their entry into the Fire, to the point that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) striving and exerting himself in calling them to faith was treated as their rescue from the Fire. His saying "Are you then going to rescue" indicates that God Most High alone is the One who has power to rescue from the Fire; no one other than Him is able to do that. Just as you cannot rescue one who has entered the Fire from the Fire, you cannot free him from what he is in, namely the deserving of punishment, by bringing about faith in him.

Chambers above chambers, built one upon another in tiers. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying "built" (mabniyyah)?

I say: its meaning, and God knows best, is that they were built in the manner of the dwellings that are on the ground, and levelled in the way that dwellings are levelled, with rivers flowing beneath them as rivers flow beneath dwellings, without any difference between the upper and the lower. "The promise of God" (wa'da Allah) is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid), because His saying "for them are chambers" carries the meaning of "God has promised them that."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verse 21:

﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾: this is rain. It has been said: all water in the earth comes from the sky, descending from it to the rock, then Allah apportions it, ﴿and makes it flow﴾, that is, causes it to enter and arranges it, ﴿as springs in the earth﴾, meaning streams, channels and watercourses, like veins in bodies. ﴿Then He brings forth thereby crops of varying colours﴾, meaning their forms: green, red, yellow, white and other hues, and their kinds: wheat, barley, sesame and others. ﴿Then it withers﴾, meaning it completes its drying out, according to al-Asma'i, because when its drying is complete it is due to be uprooted from its place of growth and to become debris, ﴿crumbled and scattered﴾ [[His words "fatatan wa darinan" (crumbled and scattered): in the Sihah, "al-darin" is the dry remains of pasture once it has aged, and it is what lies among the grass.]]. ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾, a reminder and an admonition, indicating that there must be a wise Creator, and that this occurs by determination and design, not by neglect and idleness.

It is also permissible that this be a parable for the worldly life, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of the life of this world is only like water﴾, and ﴿Present to them the example of the life of this world﴾. It has been read: "muṣfarran" (yellowed).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verse 22:

Is one whom Allah has known to be among the people of gentle kindness (luṭf), so that He showed him kindness until his breast was expanded to Islam, and he desired it and accepted it, like one who has no such kindness shown to him, whose heart is hard and constricted? ﴿Then woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah.﴾ The light of Allah is His kindness (luṭf). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, and it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the expansion of the breast?" He said: "When the light enters the heart, it expands and opens up." [[Recorded by al-Tha'labi, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. In its chain is Abu Farwa al-Rahawi, concerning whom there is some discussion.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim narrated it in al-Nawadir, in the sixth and eighty-sixth section (asl). In its chain is Ibrahim ibn [blank in the original text.], and he is weak.]] It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, then what is the sign of that?" He said: "Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death comes." This is the parallel of His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night...﴾ in the omission of the predicate, namely "from the remembrance of Allah," meaning: because of its remembrance. That is, when Allah is mentioned in their presence or His verses are recited, they recoil, and their hearts grow harder, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so it increased them in uncleanness to their uncleanness﴾. It is also read: "from (ʿan) the remembrance of Allah."

If you say: what is the difference between min (from) and ʿan (away from) here? I say: when you say "qasa qalbuhu min dhikr Allah" (his heart hardened from the remembrance of Allah), the meaning is what you have mentioned, that the hardness is because of the remembrance and on account of it. But when you say "ʿan dhikr Allah," the meaning is: he became hard and stiff, turning away from accepting the remembrance and recoiling from it. Its parallel is: "saqahu min al-ʿaymah," meaning because of his thirst, and "saqahu ʿan al-ʿaymah," meaning he gave him drink until he removed him from thirst.

Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became bored, so they said to him: "Tell us something," and this was revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of discourse﴾. The placing of the Name of Allah as the subject (mubtada') and the verb "sent down" (nazzala) in the active form serve to magnify "the best of discourse," to elevate it, to bear witness to its excellence, and to emphasize that it is ascribed to Allah and comes from Him, and that the like of it could only proceed from Him. It also alerts the reader that it is an inimitable revelation, distinct from all other discourses.

"A Book" (kitaban) is a substitute (badal) for "the best of discourse." It may also be a circumstantial accusative (hal) from it. "Consistent with itself" (mutashabihan) is unrestricted, meaning that parts of it resemble one another. It thus encompasses the similarity of its meanings in soundness and firmness, in being founded upon truth and sincerity, and in benefiting creation; the harmony of its words and their equivalence in precision and accuracy; and the correspondence of its arrangement and composition in inimitability and in silencing opponents.

"Oft-repeated" (mathani) may be an explanation (bayan) of its being "consistent with itself," since repeated narratives can only be alike. The word mathani is the plural of mathnā, meaning "repeated and reiterated," and also refers to what is repeated in its stories, reports, rulings, commands and prohibitions, promises and threats, and admonitions. It was also said: it is repeated in recitation, so it does not become tedious, as is stated in its description that it does not wear out (la yatafah) nor grow frayed (la yatashhan) [[The phrase "la yatafah wa la yatashshan": in al-Sihah, "al-tafih" means the insignificant and trifling; and "tashanat al-qirbah" means the waterskin dried out and decayed, and "tashanaj al-jild" means the skin became dry and shrivelled. (ʿ)]] and does not decay through much repetition. It may also be the plural of mathnā in the pattern mif'al, from tathniyah in the sense of repetition and reiteration, as in the verse ﴿Then return your gaze twice﴾ [67:4], meaning one repetition after another; similarly, in the expressions labbayka wa-sa'dayka and hananayka. If you ask: how can a singular be described by a plural? The answer: this is valid because the Book is a whole with detailed parts, and the details of a thing are none other than its whole. Do you not say: the Qur'an is in sevenths and fifths, and in suras and verses? Likewise you say: stories, rulings, and admonitions that are repeated. Its parallel is your saying: "The human being is bones, veins and sinews," except that you have left the qualified noun for the qualifier. Its original form is: "a Book consistent with itself, its parts oft-repeated." It is also possible to read it like your saying: "a pot of tenths" (burmatun a'shar) and "a garment of folds" (thawbun akhlaq). It is also possible that "oft-repeated" is not a qualifier, but is an accusative of specification (tamyiz) from "consistent with itself," as when you say: "I saw a man, handsome in his features" (rajulan hasanan shamā'il), the meaning being: "its repetitions are similar."

If you ask: what is the benefit of repetition and reiteration? The answer: souls are the most averse to words of admonition and advice. Thus, whatever is not repeated upon them, returning to the beginning again and again, does not settle within them nor produce its effect. For this reason, it was the custom of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to repeat what he admonished and advised them three times, or seven times [[I have not found it. In al-Bukhari, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "When he spoke a word, he would repeat it three times" — the hadith. Ahmad added: "And he would seek permission three times."]] so that it would be fixed in their hearts and planted in their breasts.

"The skin shivered" (iqsha'arra al-jild) means it contracted with a severe contraction. Its root is from the letters of qash', which is dry hide, with a fourth letter added, the ra', to make it quadriliteral and indicate an additional meaning. It is said: "his skin shivered from fear," meaning his hair stood on end [[The phrase "his hair stood on end" (waqafa sha'ruhu): meaning he stood up in terror; so in al-Sihah. (ʿ)]], and this is a metaphor for intense fear. Allah, glorified is He, may intend this as a figure of speech, portraying the extreme of their awe, or He may intend it literally. The meaning is: when they hear the Qur'an and the verses of threat, a fear afflicts them such that their skins shiver from it. Then, when they remember Allah, His mercy and His generosity in forgiveness, their skins and hearts soften, and what was in them of fear and shivering departs from them.

If you ask: what is the reason for "soften" (laina) being followed by "to" (ila)? The answer: it is made to imply a verb that takes "ila," as if it were said: "they became tranquil or settled toward the remembrance of Allah, soft and not contracted, hopeful and not fearful." If you ask: why did He mention only the remembrance of Allah without mentioning mercy? The answer: because the fundamental nature of His command is mercy and compassion, and His mercy precedes His wrath. Because His mercy is primary, when He is remembered, nothing comes to mind before any of His attributes except that He is Compassionate and Merciful.

If you ask: why did He mention the skins alone first, then join the hearts with them second? The answer: when you mention the fear whose seat is the heart, you have mentioned the hearts. So it is as if it were said: their skins shiver at the verses of threat, and their hearts fear at the first instant. Then, when they remember Allah, and the foundation of His command rests upon tenderness and mercy, they exchange the fear for hope in their hearts, and the shivering for softness in their skins.

﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides by it whom He wills﴾: "that" refers to the Book; "the guidance of Allah" means that He grants success by it to whom He wills, namely His servants who are God-fearing, so that they fear that fear and hope that hope, as He said: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [2:2]. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾ means whomever He forsakes from the wicked and the sinners, ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ [[The interpretation of "going astray" in this way is based on the Mu'tazila doctrine that God does not create evil. According to Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna), He creates it as He creates good; so "misguidance" is the creation of error in the heart. (ʿ)]]. Or, "that which occurs of fear and hope is the guidance of Allah," meaning the effect of His guidance, which is His kindness. He named it "guidance" because it comes about through guidance. ﴿He guides by it﴾, by this effect, ﴿whom He wills of His servants﴾, namely whoever keeps company with those people and sees them fearful and hopeful, so that this becomes an incentive for them to follow their conduct and walk their path. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾ means whoever His kindnesses have not affected, because of the hardness of his heart and his persistence in wickedness, ﴿for him there is no guide﴾, meaning no one at all who can have any effect upon him.

It is said: "He shielded himself with his shield," meaning he met the blow with it, protecting himself from it, and "he shielded himself with his hand." Its estimated full form is: ﴿Is one who would shield his face from the evil of the punishment﴾ [like one who is secure from the punishment]. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is 'like one who is secure,' so the predicate is omitted, as it is omitted in similar constructions, ... etc." Ahmad said: The one thrown into the Fire, may God protect us, did not intend to shield his face, but he found nothing to protect himself from the Fire except his face. Had he found something else, he would have done so. When he was flung into it face first, his condition became that of one shielding his face, so this was expressed as shielding by way of figurative representation (al-majaz al-tamthili, a metaphor by depiction of a scene), and God knows best.]] So the predicate is omitted, as it is omitted in its parallels: "the evil of the punishment" means its severity. The meaning is that when a person meets something frightening, he confronts it with his hand and seeks to guard his face with it, because the face is the most precious of his limbs to him. Whoever is thrown into the Fire is thrown with his hands chained to his neck, so he cannot shield himself from the Fire except with his face, which he had been using to shield himself from dangers with other parts of his body, as protection and defense for himself. It was said: the "face" here refers to the whole body. It was also said: the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. And the guardians of the Fire will say to them: "Taste the consequence of what you used to earn."

﴿From where they do not perceive﴾: from the direction they do not expect, and it does not occur to them that evil would come to them from it, while they were secure and carefree when they were suddenly seized from their place of safety. And "disgrace" (al-khizy) is humiliation and lowliness, such as being transformed, swallowed up by the earth, killed, or exiled, and what resembles these of God's retribution.

Qur'an in Arabic, a confirming circumstantial clause (ḥāl mu'akkada), like your saying: "Zayd came to me as a righteous man and an intelligent person." It is also permissible that it be in the accusative of praise: "free of any crookedness" (ghayra dhī ʿiwajin), meaning upright, free from contradiction and discrepancy.

If you ask: why was it not said "upright" (mustaqīman) or "not crooked" (ghayr muʿawwaj)? I answer: there are two benefits in it. The first: it negates that there is any crookedness in it at all, as in His words: ﴿and has not made in it any crookedness﴾. The second: the word ʿiwaj (crookedness) is specific to meanings, not to physical objects.

It was also said: the intended meaning of ʿiwaj is doubt and confusion. And he recited:

"And there has come to you a certainty free of crookedness ... from God, and a word not false."

[[The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and what is meant by "certainty" and "word" is the Qur'an. Or the certainty is the secrets, and the word is the Qur'an. Or the certainty is the Qur'an, and the word is what is other than it, i.e. the commands and prohibitions, and "from God" is connected to "came to you." The meaning: that (certainty) is free from doubt and confusion, and from falsehood. So "crookedness" is a clear metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya).]]

Recite to your people a parable, and say to them: What do you say of a man who is owned by several partners who are at odds and quarrel with one another, each one claiming that he is his slave? They pull him in different directions and assign him to various tasks and occupations, and when he has some need, they push him away from one another. So he is perplexed about his affair and bewildered [[Her commentary: in al-Sihah, "al-sadir" means: bewildered. (Ā)]], his heart divided by cares and his thoughts scattered, not knowing which of them is pleased with his service, or on which of them he should rely for his needs. And in another case: a man who has been surrendered wholly to one owner, and belongs to him exclusively, so he is devoted to what his service requires of him and relies on him for what sets his affairs right; his concern is single and his heart is united. Which of these two slaves is in better condition and more admirable in his circumstances?

The purpose is to depict the state of one who affirms many gods, and what follows from the premise of his doctrine: that each of them claims his worship, and they contend with one another and vie for dominance, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And some of them would overpower others﴾ [23:91]. He remains perplexed and lost, not knowing which of them he should worship, on whose lordship he should rely, from whom he should seek his provision, and from whom he should seek companionship. His mind is scattered [[Her commentary: "fahmuhu shu'a'" with a fatha means dispersed. And their saying "bihā awzā' min al-nās" means groups of people, as in al-Sihah. (Ā)]], and his heart is in fragments. And the state of one who affirms only one God is that he stands by what is required of him, knows what pleases Him and what angers Him, is favoured by Him in this world, and hopes for reward in the next.

In it (fīhi) is connected to "shurakā'" (partners), as you would say: "They share in it." And "al-tashākus" and "al-tashākhus" mean disagreement; one says: "His affairs were in disarray" (tashākasat aḥwāluhu), and "his teeth were uneven" (tashākhasat asnānuhu). ﴿A man wholly devoted [salaman] to one man﴾. It is read as "salaman" with a fatha on the lām and the ʿayn, and with fatḥa on the fā' and kasra, and with the ʿayn sukūn; these are all verbal nouns of salima. The meaning is: possessing soundness for one man, that is, wholly his, free of partnership, from their saying: "The estate became wholly his" (salimat lahu al-ḍay'a).

It is also read in the nominative (salamun) as a subject: "and there is a man wholly devoted to one man." He was made a man specifically so that he would be more discerning about what makes him wretched or happy, for a woman and a child may be heedless of this. ﴿Are the two equal in comparison?﴾ "Mathalan" is a specification of comparison (tamyīz). The meaning is: are their attributes and conditions equal? He restricted the specification to the singular only to clarify the category. It is also read as "mathalayn" (two parables), as in the verse ﴿and more abundant in wealth and children﴾ [18:34] along with ﴿stronger than them in strength﴾ [40:21]. For the one who reads "mathalayn," the pronoun in "yastawiyān" may refer to the two parables, since the implied sense is: "the likeness of a man and the likeness of a man." The meaning is: are the two equal with respect to what pertains to description, as you would say: "Two men are sufficient for them." ﴿Praise belongs to God﴾, the One who has no partner, beside every other object of worship; that is, praise must be directed to Him alone, and worship too, since it has been established that there is no god but Him. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ and so they associate others with Him.

They were waiting for the Messenger of God ﷺ to die, so He informed them that death would overtake them all, leaving no point in waiting and no basis for the survivor to gloat over the one who perishes. It is related from Qatada: "He announced to His Prophet his own death, and announced to you your own deaths." [[His statement "and announced to you your own deaths" is perhaps meant as "to them their own deaths." (ʿ)]] It was also recited as *māʾitun* and *māʾitūn*. [[Maḥmūd said: "It was recited as *innaka mayyitun* and *māʾitun*, etc." Aḥmad said: The use of *mayyit* is figurative, since the address is to the living, whereas the use of *māʾit* is literal, since the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*, "the doer") does not imply that the action is occurring at the time of address. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died He takes in their sleep﴾ (39:42), meaning: He takes the souls at the time of death (the death being the agent of taking), and He takes the one that has not died during its sleep, likening sleep to death, as in His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you back at night﴾ (6:60). So He retains those souls upon which death has been decreed in its true sense, and does not return them alive at their appointed time, and He releases the others, that is, the sleeping ones, until a term He has named, meaning He has ordained for them their true death. This is the clearest of what has been said in explaining the verse, and God knows best.]] The difference between *mayyit* and *māʾit* is that *mayyit* is a permanent, inherent attribute, like *sayyid* (lord), whereas *māʾit* is an attribute that comes about later. You say: "Zayd is *māʾit* tomorrow," just as you say, "He will be *sāʾid* (ruling) tomorrow," meaning he will die and he will rule.

When you say "Zayd is *mayyit*," it is like saying "he is *ḥayy* (alive)" in its opposite, with regard to permanence and stability. The meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ (39:30) is: you and they, and even if you are alive, you are counted among the dead, because what is certain to occur is as though it has already occurred. ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will dispute before your Lord﴾ (39:31): you and they; the second person pronoun has been given precedence over the third person pronoun, so ﴿you will dispute﴾ — you will argue against them that you delivered the message and they denied it. You strove in the call, but they persisted stubbornly, and they will make excuses with what is of no benefit. The followers will say: "We obeyed our leaders and our elders," and the leaders will say: ﴿The devils misled us, and our forefathers of old﴾.

It has been understood that the dispute is among all, and that the disbelievers dispute with one another, until it is said to them: ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾ (50:28). The believers rebuke the disbelievers with proofs, and among the People of the Qibla (Muslims) there will be disputes. ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar said: "We lived for a period of our lives thinking that this verse was revealed about us and about the People of the Book. We said: How can we dispute when our Prophet is one, our religion is one, and our Book is one? Until I saw some of us striking the faces of others with swords, and I knew that it had been revealed about us." [[Narrated by al-Ḥākim through the narration of al-Qāsim ibn ʿAwf from Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both.]] Abu Saʿid al-Khudri said: "We used to say: Our Lord is one, our Prophet is one, and our religion is one, so what is this dispute? Then, when it was the day of Ṣiffīn and some of us attacked others with swords, we said: Yes, this is it." [[Mentioned by al-Thaʿlabī, who said: Khalaf ibn Khalīfa narrated from Abū Hāshim, from al-Khudrī.]] It is related from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī: "The Companions said: How could we have a dispute when we are brothers? Then when ʿUthmān, may God be pleased with him, was killed, they said: This is our dispute." [[Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī, through the narration of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAwf from Ibrāhīm with this wording.]]

It is related from Abū al-ʿĀliya: "It was revealed concerning the People of the Qibla." The interpretation indicated by the words of God is the one I mentioned first.

Do you not see His saying: ﴿Who does greater wrong than one who lies against God and denies the truth when it comes to him?﴾ (39:32), and His saying: ﴿And the one who brings the truth and confirms it﴾ (39:33). This is nothing but an explanation and clarification of those among whom the dispute takes place. ﴿Lies against God﴾: he fabricates against Him by attributing a son and partners to Him. ﴿Denies the truth﴾: the matter which is truth itself, namely what Muḥammad ﷺ brought. ﴿When it comes to him﴾: he confronts it with denial as soon as he hears of it, without pausing, without exercising reflection or taking care to distinguish between truth and falsehood, as fair-minded people do with what they hear. ﴿An abode for the disbelievers﴾ (39:32): meaning for these people who lied against God and denied the truth. The *lām* in *lil-kāfirīn* (for the disbelievers) is a reference to them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verses 33–35:

"And the one who brings the truth and confirms it" refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): he brought the truth and believed in it, and by it he meant himself and those who follow him, just as by Moses he meant himself and his people in His saying, ﴿And indeed We gave Moses the Book, that they might be guided﴾, so He said, ﴿Those are the God-fearing﴾. The difference is that this one is in the attribute (ṣifa) and that one is in the name (ism).

It is also permissible that he means: "and the group or party who brought the truth and confirmed it," namely the Messenger who brought the truth and his companions who confirmed it. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and those who brought the truth and confirmed it." It has also been read:

"wa-ṣaddaqa bihi" (with the lighter form), meaning: people confirmed it and did not deny it to them, i.e., he conveyed it to them as it was revealed to him without distortion. It was also said: he became truthful by it, i.e., because of it, since the Qur'an is a miracle (muʿjiza), and a miracle is a confirmation from the Wise One who does not commit evil, to whoever He causes it to occur through his hand, and it is not permissible for Him to confirm other than a truthful one; so he becomes truthful by the miracle. It has also been read: "wa-ṣaddaqa bihi" (with the intensive form).

If you ask: what is the meaning of the annexation of "the worst" and "the best" to "what they did," and what is the meaning of the comparative in both? I say: as for the annexation, it is not the annexation of the superlative (afʿal) to the whole from which it is preferred, but rather the annexation of a thing to what is part of it without comparison, as when you say: "al-Ashajj is the most just of the sons of Marwan." As for the comparative, it is a notice that the evil that proceeds from them, of minor sins and slips that are expiated, is for them the "worst," because of their great regard for disobedience; and the good they do is, in the sight of Allah, the "best," because of the sincerity of their intention in it. Therefore He mentioned their evil with "the worst" and their good with "the best." It has also been read: "aswāʾ alladhī ʿamilū," as the plural of sūʾ (evil).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verse 36–37:

﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ The interrogative hamza of denial (hamzat al-inkar) has been placed before the negative particle, so it conveys the meaning of affirming sufficiency and establishing it.

It is also read: "bi-kaafin ʿabdahu" (with a kaaf and ʿabdahu), where "His servant" refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); and "bi-kaafin ʿibadahu" (His servants), meaning the prophets. The reason is that the Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We fear that our gods will afflict you with madness (takhbalaka), and we fear for you their harm (maʿarratuha) because of your reviling of them." [Note: "maʿarratuha" means its sin, as stated in al-Sihah (ʿAyn).]

It is narrated that he (ﷺ) sent Khalid to al-ʿUzza to break her. Her custodian (sadin) said to him: "I warn you, O Khalid, that she has a power against which nothing can stand." Khalid went to her and smashed her nose. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His prophet, to protect him from every evil and to ward off from him every calamity in places of fear?﴾ In this there is a mockery of them, for they frightened him with that which cannot bring benefit or harm.

Or: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His prophets?﴾ Their peoples said something similar, and Allah sufficed them. This is the saying of the people of Hud: ﴿We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud 11:54].

It is permissible that He means: the servant and the servants in general, because He is sufficient for them in hardships and the one who takes charge of their affairs.

It is also read: "bi-kaafin ʿibadahu" (with the genitive construction). And "wa-yukafi ʿibadahu" / "wa-yukaafi ʿibadahu": it may be non-hamzated, a form of mufaʿala from sufficiency (kifaya), like your saying "yujazi" for "yujziy"; and it is more emphatic than "kafa," because it is built on the form of intensification. And al-mubaraah (contending/rivalry) is that it be hamzated, from al-mukafaʾah, which is recompense, due to what preceded in His saying: ﴿and He will reward them their wage﴾ [39:35].

﴿with those besides Him﴾: He means the idols they took as gods besides Him. ﴿Who is Mighty﴾: invincible, unassailable; ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾: He takes vengeance upon His enemies. In this is a warning to the Quraysh and a promise to the believers that He will avenge them upon them and give them victory over them.

If you ask: why did he pose the question to himself rather than to them? I answer: because they frightened him with the harm of the idols and their power to afflict. So he was commanded to first establish with them that the Creator of the world is God alone. Then, after this establishment, he says to them: If the Creator of the world, whom you have acknowledged, wills for me a harm, by way of illness, poverty, or other calamities, or a mercy, by way of health, wealth, or the like, are these whom you have frightened me with "uncovering His harm" or "withholding His mercy"? Until, when he has silenced them and cut them off so that they cannot utter a word, he says: "God is sufficient for me" (meaning sufficient against the harm of your idols), "upon Him do the trusting trust." And there is mockery in this. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked them and they fell silent, and then the verse "Say: God is sufficient for me" was revealed.

If you ask: why was the feminine form used, "kāshifāt" and "mumsikāt," after the words of the Exalted, "and they frighten you with those besides Him"? I answer: He made them feminine because they were females, namely al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat. God the Exalted said: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other? Is the male for you and the female for Him?" This is to weaken them and to render them more incapable, an added weakening and incapacitating, with respect to what he demanded of them, namely the uncovering of harm and the withholding of mercy, because femininity belongs to the category of softness and laxity, just as masculinity belongs to the category of strength and firmness. It is as if he said: the females who are al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are weaker than what you claim for them and more incapable. And there is mockery in this too.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verse 42:

"Al-anfus" as it is (the phrase is kept as it stands). Wa-tawaffa-ha: its causing to die (imatatuha), which is that there is stripped away from it that by which it is living, sensing and perceiving:

from the soundness of its parts and its wholeness, for when soundness is stripped away, it is as though its very self has been stripped away. "Wa-allati lam tamut fi manamiha": he means "and He takes the souls that have not died in their sleep," i.e., He takes them at the time they sleep, likening the sleepers to the dead.

From this is His saying, ﴿And it is He who takes you back at night﴾, where they do not discern and do not act, just as the dead are likewise. "Fa-yumsiku al-anfus allati qada 'alayha al-mawt": ﴿He keeps back those souls on which He has decreed death﴾, i.e., He does not return them alive at their time, "wa-yursilu al-ukhra": ﴿and sends the others back﴾, the sleeping ones, "ila ajalin musamma": ﴿until a term appointed﴾, i.e., until the time He has set for their death.

It has been said: "Yatawaffa al-anfus" means He fully receives them and completes them, and these are the souls in which life and movement are present; and "yatawaffa al-anfus allati lam tamut fi manamiha" refers to the souls of discernment. They said: what is taken in sleep is the soul of discernment, not the soul of life, because if the soul of life departs, the soul departs with it, and the sleeper breathes. They related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) concerning the son of Adam: "a soul and a spirit," between which is a likeness of the sunbeam: the soul is that by which there is reason and discernment, and the spirit is that by which there is life and movement; so when the servant sleeps, Allah takes his soul and does not take his spirit. [[I have not found it.]]

The correct view is what I mentioned first, because Allah, Mighty and Exalted, attached the taking, the death and the sleep all together to the souls, and those who spoke of the soul of life and movement and the soul of reason and discernment did not mean something that is characterized by death and sleep; rather, it is the body (al-jumla) that dies and it is that which sleeps.

﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾: indeed in the taking of souls, in their being dead and sleeping, and in their being kept back and sent until a term, are signs of Allah's power and knowledge, ﴿for a people who reflect﴾, who turn their thoughts over in it and take lesson.

And it was recited: "qada 'alayha al-mawt" (with the verb in the passive form).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verses 43–44:

"Or have they taken" — rather, the Quraysh have taken — "intercessors besides Allah," that is, without His permission. The interrogative hamza here is for denunciation (inkar). They said: "These are our intercessors with Allah," yet no one intercedes with Him except by His permission.

Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: To Allah belongs all intercession﴾? That is, He is its owner, so no one can intercede except under two conditions: that the one for whom intercession is made is one whom He approves, and that the intercessor is one who has been given permission. Here both conditions are absent altogether.

"Even though they" — its meaning: "Would they intercede even though they" — ﴿possess nothing and do not understand﴾. That is: even if they were in this state, possessing nothing at all, so that they could own intercession, and having no understanding.

﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a confirmation of His saying ﴿To Allah belongs all intercession﴾, because if the whole dominion is His, and intercession is part of dominion, then He is its owner.

If you ask: with what does His saying ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾ connect? I say: with what immediately precedes it. Its meaning: to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth today, and then to Him you will be returned on the Day of Resurrection, so that on that Day dominion belongs to none but Him. Thus He possesses the dominion of this world and the Hereafter.

The meaning turns on His words "alone" (wahdahu), that is: when God alone is mentioned and their gods are not mentioned along with Him, they are repulsed (ishmaza), that is:

they recoil and are constricted. "And when those besides Him are mentioned," who are their gods, whether God is mentioned along with them or not, they rejoice (istabshara), because of their infatuation with them and their forgetting the right of God, which is more important than them. It was said: when it is said "There is no god but God, alone, with no partner," they recoil, because it contains a negation of their gods. It was also said: he meant their rejoicing at what the tongue of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) produced of mentioning their gods when he recited "By the star" (al-Najm) at the door of the Ka'bah, so they prostrated with him out of their joy. The rejoicing and the repulsion are contrasted, since each of them is the extreme in its category: rejoicing is that his heart is filled with delight until the surface of his face is expanded and brightens, while repulsion is that he is filled with grief and rage until the constriction appears on the skin of his face. If you ask: what is the governing element (al-'amil) of "idha dhukira" (when it is mentioned)? I say: the governing element in "idha" is the sudden-occurrence sense (al-mufaja'ah), its implied sense being "at the time those besides Him are mentioned, they suddenly rejoice."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verse 46:

[The Prophet (ﷺ) was bewildered (ba'l) by them, and by the sheer stubbornness of their disbelief and obstinacy. (Lexicographers note: in al-Sihah, "ba'l al-rajul" with a kasra means he was dumbfounded, i.e. astonished.) (ʿAn)]

So he was told: Call upon Allah by His greatest names, and say: You alone are able to judge between me and them, and no one else has any means against them. This contains a description of their condition, an excuse for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), consolation for him, and a warning to them. It is related from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym (in al-Nasafi: Khaythim), who used to speak little, that when he was informed of the killing of al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, and he was angered at his killer, the people said: Now he will speak. He said nothing more than: "Alas! Have they really done it?" and then he recited this verse. And it is narrated that he said after this: "Killed is the one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to seat on his lap and place his mouth upon his mouth."

And there appeared to them from Allah a threat (wa'īd) against them whose severity and intensity cannot be described, and this is the counterpart of His saying, concerning the promise, ﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them﴾. The meaning is: there appeared to them, from the wrath of Allah and His punishment, what had never been in their reckoning and what their souls had not imagined. It was also said: they did deeds that they reckoned to be good deeds, but then they were bad deeds. It is narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri that he recited it and said: "Woe to the people of showing off (riya'), woe to the people of showing off." Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir grieved at his death, and it was said to him, and he said: "I fear a verse from the Book of Allah," and he recited it: ﴿And there will appear to them the evil of what they earned﴾. "So I fear that there will appear to me from Allah what I had not reckoned."

﴿And there will appear to them the evils of what they earned﴾: that is, the evils of their deeds which they earned. Or the evils of their earning, when their records are presented and they were hidden from them, like His saying ﴿Allah has counted it, and they have forgotten it﴾. Or he intended by the evils: the kinds of punishment by which they are requited for what they earned, and so He called them evils, as He said ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

﴿And there encompassed them﴾: it descended upon them and surrounded them, the requital of their mockery.
