The Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) notes in the text are rendered in the same brackets.

Al-takhwil (conferring a favour): it is specific to bounty. One says *khawwalani* when he gives you without recompense. "On knowledge" means: on my knowledge that I would be given it, because of the merit and deservingness in me. Or it means: on God's knowledge of me and of my deservingness. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is 'on knowledge from God about me and my deservingness...' etc." Ahmad said: Thus he says, according to my measure, wishing that God would reward him in the Hereafter. The difference between praise in this world and praise in the Hereafter is that praise in this world is obligatory upon the servant, because it is for a blessing bestowed upon him by grace. Praise in the Hereafter is not obligatory upon him, because it is for a blessing that is obligatory upon God, mighty and majestic. God spoke truly when He said: ﴿And it is a trial﴾. Only the People of the Sunnah are saved from it, for they believe that reward is by God's bounty and mercy, not by deservingness, and they follow in this the saying of the master of mankind (ﷺ): "No one enters Paradise by his deeds." It was said: "Not even you, Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God envelops me with His mercy." How foolish is the one who deceives himself, sets his head on its course, and hopes that Paradise is owed to him by God.]] Or it means: on my knowledge of the ways of earning, as Qarun said: ﴿I was given it only on knowledge I have﴾ (28:78).

If you ask: why is the pronoun mentioned in *utituhu* (I was given it), when it refers to the blessing? I answer: it is by consideration of the meaning, because His saying *ni'matan minna* (a blessing from Us) means some of the blessings and a portion of them. It is also possible that *ma* in *innama* is a relative pronoun, not an exclusive particle, so that the pronoun returns to it, meaning: that which I have been given is on knowledge.

*Bal hiya fitnah* (Nay, it is a trial) is a rejection of his statement, as if He said: We did not confer on you what you say; rather, it is a trial and a test for you: will you be grateful or will you be ungrateful?

If you ask: how is the pronoun mentioned and then made feminine? I answer: it is by consideration of the meaning at first, and by consideration of the wording at the end. Also, since the predicate is feminine, namely *fitnah*, it was permissible to make the subject feminine on its account, because it has the same meaning, as in their saying *ma ja'at hajatuka* (your need did not come). It is also read *bal huwa fitnah* (Nay, it is a trial), in agreement with *innama utitu-hu*.

If you ask: what is the reason that this verse is joined with *fa* (then), while a similar verse at the beginning of the surah is joined with *waw* (and)? I answer: the reason is that this verse is the consequence of His saying ﴿And when God alone is mentioned, their hearts recoil﴾ (39:45). [[Mahmud said: "If you ask: why was this verse joined to the one before it with *fa*, while the verse before it at the beginning of the surah is joined with *waw*? He answered that this verse is the consequence of His saying 'And when God alone is mentioned...' etc." Ahmad said: A splendid statement; understand it, for it is more than a few such comparisons.]] It means that they recoil from the remembrance of God and rejoice in the remembrance of the gods. So when harm touches one of them, he calls upon the one from whose remembrance he recoiled, not the one in whose remembrance he rejoiced. What lies between them is an *i'tiraD* (parenthetical interjection).

If you ask: the proper thing for a parenthetical clause is that the speaker should emphasise it between it and what it interrupts [[His saying "the speaker between it and it" — perhaps "and it" is an addition by one of the copyists. (A)]]. I answer: in the parenthetical clause there is the Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication to his Lord, by a command from Him, and His saying ﴿You judge between Your servants﴾ (39:46), and then what follows it of great threat. This is an emphasis on the denial of their recoiling and rejoicing, and of their returning to God in hardships and not to their gods. It is as if it were said: "Say, O Lord: none judges between me and these people who dare against You with such audacity, and commit such an evil, except You." His saying ﴿And if those who did wrong had all that is in the earth, and the like of it with it﴾ (39:47) applies to them and to every wrongdoer if it is taken in its generality, or to them specifically if you mean them by it. It is as if it were said: "And if these wrongdoers had all that is in the earth, and the like of it with it, they would ransom themselves with it, when I pass upon them the evil of the punishment." These subtleties and fine points are revealed only by the science of the arrangement (*'ilm al-nazm*, the science of Qur'anic composition), and otherwise they remain hidden within their sheaths.

As for the first verse, it is not the consequence of anything; it is merely a sentence that corresponds to the sentence before it, so it was joined to it with *waw*, as when you say: "Zayd stood up and 'Amr sat down."

If you ask: in what respect is it a consequence? Recoiling from the remembrance of God does not necessitate their turning to Him; rather it necessitates their turning away from Him. I answer: there is subtlety in this causal link. Its explanation is that you say: "Zayd believes in God; when harm touches him he turns to Him." This is a clear consequence with no ambiguity. Then you say: "Zayd disbelieves in God; when harm touches him he turns to Him," and you bring it with *fa* as you bring it there. It is as if the disbeliever, when he turns to God in the way the believer turns to Him, places his unbelief in the position of faith and treats it as the cause of turning. So you are relating what the disbeliever has inverted. Do you not see that by this speech you intend denial and wonder at his action?

The pronoun in qālahā refers back to his saying "innamā ūtītuhu ʿalā ʿilm" (I was given it only on account of knowledge), because it is a word or a sentence of speech.

It is also read qad qālahu, in the sense of "the saying" and "the statement." Those who came before them are Qarun and his people, when he said: "I was given it only on knowledge I possess," and his people were content with it, so it is as though they said it themselves. It is also permissible that among the earlier nations there were others who said the same thing. "Their earnings did not avail them" refers to the goods of this world that they acquired and amassed. "Those of these" refers to the polytheists of your people. "It will strike them," like what struck those (earlier ones): their chiefs were killed at Badr, and provision was withheld from them, so they suffered drought for seven years; then it was extended to them and they were given rain for seven years. Then it was said to them: "Did they not know that none withholds and none extends (provision) except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?"

Those who have transgressed against themselves (أَسْرَفُوا عَلى أَنْفُسِهِمْ): they have wronged themselves by excess in sins and going to extremes in them. Do not despair (لا تَقْنَطُوا): it is read with a fatha, a kasra and a damma on the nun. Indeed Allah forgives all sins (إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعاً): meaning, on condition of repentance.

[[His statement "meaning, on condition of repentance": when one repents, the generality includes shirk; and when there is no repentance, there is no forgiveness of grave sins according to the Mu'tazilah. It is permissible (that forgiveness comes) through intercession and through sheer grace according to the Ahl al-Sunnah. "Indeed Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" (﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَغْفِرُ أَنْ يُشْرَكَ بِهِ وَيَغْفِرُ ما دُونَ ذلِكَ لِمَنْ يَشاءُ﴾), as is established in the science of tawhid (ʿilm al-tawhid, the science of divine oneness): refer to it. (ʿ)]]

This condition has been mentioned repeatedly in the Qur'an, so its mention in the places where it is stated serves as a mention of it in the places where it is not stated, because the Qur'an is in the ruling of a single speech, and contradiction is not permissible in it. In the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud: "Indeed Allah forgives all sins for whomever He wills" (﴿يغفر الذنوب جميعا لمن يشاء﴾). By "whomever He wills" is meant the one who repents, because the will of Allah follows His wisdom and justice, not His sovereignty and dominion. It has been said that in the reading of the Prophet (ﷺ) and Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her): "Indeed Allah forgives all sins and does not mind" (﴿يغفر الذنوب جميعا ولا يبالى﴾). Parallel to the negation of concern is the negation of fear in His statement, Exalted is He, "and He does not fear its consequence" (﴿وَلا يَخافُ عُقْباها﴾).

It has been said: the people of Makkah said, "Muhammad claims that whoever worships idols and kills a soul that Allah has forbidden will not be forgiven; so how (can that be), when we did not emigrate, though we worshipped idols and killed the soul that Allah has forbidden?" Then this was revealed. It is narrated that ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿah and al-Walid ibn al-Walid and a group with them embraced Islam, then they were tried and tortured, so they apostatized. We used to say: "Allah will never accept from them any repentance or ransom, ever." Then this was revealed. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote it to them, so they embraced Islam and emigrated. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him).

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I would not love that I had the world and what is in it in exchange for this verse." A man said, "O Messenger of Allah, and whoever associates partners (with Allah)?" He was silent for a while, then said, "Unquestionably, and whoever associates partners (with Allah)," three times.

[[Narrated by al-Tabari, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab, in the forty-seventh (chapter), from the hadith of Thawban. In its chain is Ibn Lahiʿah from Abu Qubayl, and both are weak.]]

And turn back in repentance to your Lord, and submit to Him, and sincerely devote your deeds to Him. He mentioned turning back (inabah) right after forgiveness so that no one would hope to obtain it without repentance, and to indicate that it is a necessary condition for it, which is not attained without it. ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, like His saying ﴿those who listen to the word and follow its best﴾. ﴿While you do not perceive﴾: that is, it will come upon you while you are heedless, as if you feared nothing because of the extent of your negligence and forgetfulness, ﴿lest a soul should say﴾, out of dislike that it should say. If you ask: why is "soul" indefinite? I answer: because what is meant is some of the souls, namely the soul of the disbeliever. It is also permissible that what is meant is a soul distinguished from other souls, either by its extreme obstinacy in disbelief, or by a great punishment. It is also permissible that the meaning is "a multitude," as al-A'sha said:

"And many a open space, if I called out to its tall ones [al-hu], a noble man would come to me, shaking his head in anger."

[He called his people around me, and they came to his aid, and I called to a people behind the embankment, cowardly.

And many a open space, if I called out to its tall ones, a noble man would come to me, shaking his head in anger.

By al-A'sha. It is said it belongs to Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', describing his people as cowardly, to the point that they are like dead buried ones, the stones having become a mound (musannah) over them. "Sanaytu al-shay'" means I made the thing easy, i.e., made it smooth and levelled, or worn and crumbled. It is also permissible that its origin is musannah, so the second nun was changed to an alif. "Sannantu al-hajar" means I sharpened the stone and smoothed it. Describing graves with this is hyperbole in describing his people's cowardice; rather, they are inferior to those dead. So "rubba buqay'" means a place in which there are many kinds of trees, and what is meant is a cemetery, not Baqi' al-Gharqad, which is specifically the cemetery of Madinah, "if I called out to its tall ones," that is, if I called their bravest, a noble man would come to me shaking his head from the dust of the grave, or from anger at the harm that befell me. What is meant is not one noble man, but many nobles, as the context indicates. "Al-hu" with the unpointed ha means the brave one; with the pointed kha it means honey; with the jim it means what is raised and thick from the earth.]

He means: troops of nobles who would support him, not one noble man. Its parallel: "many a land I have crossed, and many a hero I have fought." He has snatched the thrust while intending only the multitude. It was read "yā ḥasratī" according to the original form, and "yā ḥasratāy" combining the replacement with what it replaces.

And al-janb (side) means the side; it is said: "I am in the side (janb), the flank (jānib) and the vicinity (nāḥiya) of so-and-so," and "so-and-so is gentle in side and flank." Then they said: "he neglected in his side and his flank," meaning in his right. Sabiq al-Barbari said:

"Will you not fear God regarding a loving one, who has a burning liver that is cut by you? [Will you not fear God regarding a loving one, who has a burning liver torn by you?

A stranger, longing, enamoured with remembering you, and every stranger far from home is enamoured with longing.]

This is by Jamil ibn Ma'mar, seeking the sympathy of his beloved Buthayna and lamenting to her what befell him concerning her. That is: will you not fear God regarding a loving one, i.e., regarding his right which is incumbent upon you. So "janb" is a metonymy for that. "Al-wamiq" is the one of intense love, meaning himself. "Hurra" means one with heat and burning. "Taqatta'" originally is "tataqatta'," and "al-idkar" originally is "al-idhtikar," its tā' changed to a dal, and the dhal with a dot was assimilated into it; he addressed her with the plural masculine form out of reverence. In the verse is the reversal of the last part onto the first, which is among the wonders of speech.

This is from the category of metonymy (kināya), for when you establish a matter in the place and domain of a man, you have established it in him. Do you not see his saying:

"Generosity, manliness and liberality are in a tent pitched over the son of al-Hashraj."

[This is by Ziyad al-A'jam praising Abd Allah ibn al-Hashraj, governor of Nishapur; it is of the type of metonymy intended to indicate attribution, meaning that he is specially characterized by these qualities, which are not found in anyone else, and there is no tent there nor any pitching at all.]

From it is the people's saying: "for your sake (li-makanika) I did such and such," meaning: for your sake. And in the hadith: "Among hidden shirk is that a man prays for the sake of (li-makan) another man." [Narrated by Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Bazzar, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi, from the narration of Rabih ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Sa'id from his father from his grandfather, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ came out to us one day while we were discussing the Dajjal. He said: 'Something other than the Dajjal is what I fear for you more: the hidden shirk, that a man acts for the sake of a man.'" This is the wording of al-Hakim.]

Likewise: "I did this on your behalf (min jihatika)." Thus, since no difference remains, in terms of achieving the purpose, between mentioning the place and omitting it, it is said: ﴿I neglected in the side of God﴾, in the sense of: "I neglected regarding the essence of God." If you ask: then your statement returns to the point that mentioning the side is no different from not mentioning it, apart from what it gives of the beauty of metonymy and its eloquence, so it is as if it were said: "I neglected regarding God." Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verse 60:

They lied against Allah, ascribing to Him what is not permissible for Him, the Exalted. [[Mahmud said: "That is, those who ascribed to Him, may He be exalted, what is not permissible for Him, He being exalted above it..." etc.]] Ahmad said: He has gone beyond the bounds of tafsir (exegesis) because of a sickness in his heart for which there is no cure except the success (tawfiq) that was denied to him, and from which none can heal him except the One who decreed this misguidance for him and made it certain. We shall impose upon him the penalty of refutation, since he has uncovered his face. Had it not been for the condition of this book, we would have turned away from him entirely and averted our side from him. With Allah is success. So we say: As for his insinuation that the Sunnis believe that ugly acts are from Allah, the Exalted, he answers it with their belief, to which the Exalted's saying after some verses of this surah refers: ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is Guardian over all things﴾ (39:62). As for al-Zamakhshari and his brethren, the Qadariyya, they alter the meaning of this verse and say: He is not the Creator of all things, because ugly acts are things and are not created by Him.

Thus they believed that they had declared Him free from imperfection, whereas they had in fact committed shirk. As for his insinuation against them that they permit Him to create a creation without purpose, that is because His acts, may He be exalted, are not subject to causation, for He is the Doer of what He wills. But according to the Qadariyya, He is not a Doer of what He wills, because an act either contains wisdom and benefit, in which case it is obligatory upon Him to perform it according to them, or it is devoid of them, in which case it is obligatory upon Him not to perform it. Then where is the effect of will? As for his belief that imposing what cannot be borne is an injustice to Allah, the Exalted, that is a false belief, because that follows only as a necessary consequence of their belief that Allah, the Exalted, is the Creator of His servants' acts. Then imposing those acts is imposing what is not created by them. The first premise is true, and the necessary consequence of truth is true. Injustice has no meaning except disposing of another's property without his permission, and the servants are the property of Allah, the Exalted. So how can true injustice be conceived from Him? Exalted is Allah above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation (﴿17:43﴾).

As for his insinuation that they permit Him to inflict pain without compensation, it is said to him: What do you say, O suspect, concerning the infliction of pain upon animals and children, which have no compensation, and which is not consequent upon a prior desert? This is unlike the Qadariyya, who say that there must be a prior desert or compensation for pain. As for his belief that permitting the vision of Allah, the Exalted, entails belief in corporeality, that is a deception arising from his trust in the rational proofs that permit it, together with his disavowal of belief in corporeality. He did not realize that it is confronted by the guidance of the words of the Prophet of guidance (peace and blessings be upon him): "Indeed you will see your Lord as you see the moon on the night of its fullness, and you will not be harmed (or crowded) in seeing Him." This is an explicit text which rejects interpretation, and nothing of exaggeration deters the one who holds to it.

As for his saying that they take cover behind "bilakfa," he means by it their saying "without how" (bila kayf). Indeed, it is a cover that the hand of falsehood, cut short, cannot tear away, and the blind eye of error cannot keep far from guidance.

As for his insinuation that they make rivals to Allah by affirming with Him eternal attributes, that is a denial of their affirmation of the attributes of perfection. No, by Allah, what made rivals to Allah were the Qadariyya, when they made themselves create what they desire and wish, contrary to the will of their Lord, to the extent that they said: "What they willed came to be, and what Allah willed does not come to be." As for the Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni tradition), they added nothing beyond believing that Allah has knowledge, power, will, hearing, sight, speech and life, as reason indicates and revelation has reported. And what refuge does the Qadari have when he hears the saying of Allah, ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ (7:89), except to believe that Allah has knowledge, or to deny the signs of Allah and extinguish His light? But Allah refuses except to perfect His light, though the disbelievers dislike it (﴿9:32﴾).

As for his saying that they affirm for Allah, the Exalted, a hand, a leg and a face, that is a slander beyond doubt, and none of the Ahl al-Sunna has said this. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr affirmed only the scriptural attributes that occur in the Qur'an: the two hands, the two eyes, and the face, and he did not exceed in affirming them what has occurred in the Book of the Mighty. Moreover, others among the Ahl al-Sunna interpreted the two hands as power and bounty, and the face as the Essence, and this has passed in several places of the book. He has, in this dispute, taken on the condition of one who digs with his hoof into his own death, and his exposing of his corrupt belief to the uncovering of his cover and its disclosure. What compelled me to harshness in addressing him is anger for the sake of Allah, His Messenger (ﷺ), and the Ahl al-Sunna, for he has transgressed in his manners toward them and, by his lie, has carried them to lying. And with Allah is success.

[[The commentary (of al-Zamakhshari) continues:]] against Him, so they attributed to Him a child and a partner, and said: "These are our intercessors," and said: ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ (43:20), and said: ﴿Allah has commanded us to do it﴾ (7:28). "No evil touches them" means He saves them by negating evil and grief from them. Or [it means] by the cause of their salvation, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not think them to be in a mafāza from the punishment﴾, that is, in a place of safety from it, since salvation is among the greatest success. **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 39, verses 62–63:**

﴿لَهُ مَقَالِيدُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾: that is, He is the owner of their affairs and their keeper. This is a *kinayah* (metonymy, an allusive expression), because the one who guards the treasuries and manages their affairs is the one who holds their *maqalid* (keys). From this come the expressions "So-and-so was handed the keys of kingship" (*ألقيت إليه مقاليد الملك*). *Maqalid* means keys, and it has no singular form from its own root. It is also said *miqlid*, and it is said *iqlid* and *aqalid*. The word is originally Persian. If you ask, "What has the clear Arabic Book to do with Persian?" I answer: Arabicization (*ta'rib*) made it Arabic, just as usage removes a word from being meaningless (*muhmal*).

If you ask, "With what is His saying ﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ connected?" I answer: it is connected to His saying ﴿وَيُنَجِّي اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا بِمَفَازَتِهِمْ﴾ (And Allah will deliver those who feared Him to their place of success), meaning: Allah delivers the God-fearing by their attainment of success, and ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا هُمُ الْخَاسِرُونَ﴾ (those who disbelieved, they are the losers).

Between the two statements there is an interjection: He is the Creator of all things and the Guardian over them. Nothing of the deeds of the responsible (*mukallafin*) is hidden from Him, nor of the recompense they deserve for them. It has also been said that it is connected to what follows it, meaning that everything in the heavens and the earth has Allah as its Creator and the Opener of its door (*fatih babihi*), and ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ means those who denied and rejected that matter is so, ﴿أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْخَاسِرُونَ﴾.

It is also reported: Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the interpretation of His saying ﴿لَهُ مَقَالِيدُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, and he said: "O Uthman, no one has asked me about it before you. Its interpretation is: *la ilaha illa Allah*, *Allahu akbar*, *subhan Allah wa bihamdihi*, *astaghfir Allah*, *wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah*. This is a *kinayah* (metonymy, an allusive expression), because the one who guards the treasuries and manages their affairs is the one who holds their *maqalid* (keys). From this come the expressions "So-and-so was handed the keys of kingship" (*ألقيت إليه مقاليد الملك*). *Maqalid* means keys, and it has no singular form from its own root. It is also said *miqlid*, and it is said *iqlid* and *aqalid*. The word is originally Persian. If you ask, "What has the clear Arabic Book to do with Persian?" I answer: Arabicization (*ta'rib*) made it Arabic, just as usage removes a word from being meaningless (*muhmal*).

If you ask, "With what is His saying ﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ connected?" I answer: it is connected to His saying ﴿وَيُنَجِّي اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا بِمَفَازَتِهِمْ﴾ (And Allah will deliver those who feared Him to their place of success), meaning: Allah delivers the God-fearing by their attainment of success, and ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا هُمُ الْخَاسِرُونَ﴾ (those who disbelieved, they are the losers).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verse 64:

"Afaghayra Allahi" (﴿Is it other than God that I should worship?﴾) is in the accusative, governed by "a'budu" (I worship). "Ta'murunni" (you command me) is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraz). Its meaning is: "Is it other than God that I worship by your command?" This is because the polytheists said to him: "Touch some of our gods and we will believe in your God."

Or, "afaghayra" may be governed by what is indicated by the clause "ta'murunni a'budu" (you command me, I worship), since it carries the sense of "ta'buduni" (you worship me) and "taqulluna li: u'bud" (you say to me: worship). The original form is "ta'murunni an a'bud" (you command me that I worship), so the particle "an" (that) is elided and the verb is put in the nominative, as in the line of poetry:

"Ala ayyuha al-zajiri ahdara al-wagha" [[The explanation of this evidence has been given in the first volume, page 159, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

Do you not see that you say: "Afaghayra Allahi taqulluna li u'buduhu" (Is it other than God that you say to me, worship it?) and "Afaghayra Allahi taqulluna li a'bud" (Is it other than God that you say to me, I worship?). Likewise, "Afaghayra Allahi ta'murunni an a'buduhu" (Is it other than God that you command me to worship it?) and "Afaghayra Allahi ta'murunni an a'bud" (Is it other than God that you command me that I worship?). The evidence for the soundness of this reading is the reading of the one who read "a'budu" in the accusative. It is also read "ta'murunni," according to the original form, and "ta'murunni," with the assimilation or elision of the nun.

Readings: "Layuḥbiṭanna ʿamaluka" and "Layuḥbiṭanna" are read in the passive voice (ʿalā al-binā' lil-mafʿūl). "Lanuḥbiṭanna," with the nūn and the yā' (i.e., "Yuḥbiṭanna"), meaning: "Layuḥbiṭanna Allāh" (God will nullify), or "al-shirk" (the association of partners).

If you say: the ones to whom revelation was addressed are a group, so how does He say "If you associate" (la'in ashraka) in the singular? I say: its meaning is, "It was revealed to you: if you associate, your deeds will surely be nullified; and to those before you, the like of it." Or: "It was revealed to you and to each one of them: if you associate," as you say, "He clothed us a robe," meaning each one of us.

If you say: what is the difference between the two lāms? I say: the first is the lām muwaṭṭi'a (preparatory lām) for the implied oath, and the second is the lām of the response (lām al-jawāb). This response takes the place of both responses, namely the response of the oath and the response of the condition.

If you say: how is this statement valid, given that God Most High knows that His messengers do not associate and their deeds are not nullified? I say: it is on the basis of supposition (ʿalā sabīl al-farḍ), and impossibilities may be supposed for purposes, so how much more so what is not impossible. Do you not see His saying: "And if your Lord had willed, all those on earth would have believed, all of them together" (Q. 10:99), meaning by way of compulsion; but that will not happen, because of the absence of the motive toward it and the presence of what turns away from it.

If you say: what is the meaning of His saying: "And you will surely be among the losers" (wa-latakūnanna min al-khāsirīn)? I say: it may mean: "you will surely be among the losers" because of the nullification of the deed. It may also mean: "you will surely be in the Hereafter among the number of the losers who have lost themselves, if you die in apostasy." It is also permissible that God's anger toward the Messenger be greater, so that He would not give him respite after apostasy. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: "Then We would have made you taste double of life and double of death" (Q. 17:75). "Rather, worship God" (bal Allāha fa-ʿbud) is a rejection of what they urged him to do, namely to touch some of their gods (istilām baʿḍ ālihatihim). It is as if He said: "Do not worship what they command you to worship; rather, if you are an intelligent person, worship God." So the condition is omitted, and the fronting of the object is made a substitute for it. [[Maḥmūd said: "The original statement is: 'If you are a worshipper, then worship God,' the condition is omitted, and the fronting of the object is made a substitute for it. End of his words."

Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: What is implied by Sībawayh's statement regarding such verses is that the original is "fa-ʿbud Allāh," then the first verb was omitted for brevity. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 39, verse 67:

When something great is truly known by a person, and he estimates it in himself at its true measure, he magnifies it as it truly deserves to be magnified. Therefore it was said: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾. It is also read with the intensive form (tashdid), meaning: they did not magnify Him with the full reality of magnification. Then He drew their attention to His greatness and the majesty of His station through the method of takhyil (figurative imagination, representation), so He said: ﴿The earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾. The purpose of this statement, if you take it as it is, in its entirety and as a whole, is to depict His greatness and to make people stop before the reality of His majesty, and nothing else, without taking the handful or the right hand toward a literal sense or a figurative sense. [[Mahmud said: "The purpose of this statement is to depict His greatness, exalted is He, and to make people stop before the reality of His majesty, without taking the handful or the right hand toward a literal direction or a figurative direction. Likewise is the ruling concerning what is narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: that a rabbi came to him and said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, indeed God holds the heavens on the Day of Resurrection on one finger, and the earths on one finger, and the mountains on one finger, and the trees on one finger, and all the rest of creation on one finger, then He shakes them and says: I am the King.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed and was amazed at what the rabbi said, then he recited this verse in confirmation of him. The most eloquent of the Arabs laughed only because he understood from it nothing but what the scholars of rhetoric understand, without picturing a holding, a shaking, or anything of that sort. Rather, his understanding of it, from first to last, settled upon the essence and the core, which is the indication of overwhelming power, which the listener cannot reach to stand upon except by putting the expression in this method of takhyil. Then he said: 'Most of the speech of the prophets and the heavenly books, and their essence, is takhyil, in which feet have slipped since ancient times.' End of his words." This is supported by what is in al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, so it is noted in the margin. It is also supported by "O Abu al-Qasim," which was the custom of the Jews in addressing him ﷺ. [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. "Note": it occurred to him that it was Gabriel, which is an error in transcription. What is in the Sahih is "a rabbi of the Jews came," and in another narration "that a Jew," and in another narration "that a man of the People of the Book."]] The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed in wonder at what he said, then recited in confirmation of him: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ ... the verse. The most eloquent of the Arabs ﷺ laughed and was amazed only because he did not understand from it anything but what the scholars of rhetoric understand, without imagining a holding, a finger, a shaking, or anything of that sort. Rather, his understanding of it, from first to last, settled upon the essence and the core, which is the indication of overwhelming power, and that great acts, in which understandings and minds are bewildered and which imaginations cannot grasp, are easy for Him with an ease that the listener cannot reach to stand upon except by putting the expression in this method of takhyil. You will not find a chapter in the science of rhetoric more subtle, finer, or more gentle than this chapter, nor more beneficial or helpful in pursuing the interpretation of the ambiguous passages of God's speech in the Qur'an, the other heavenly books, and the words of the prophets, for most of it, and its bulk, [[His saying "and its bulk": that is, its greater part. (Ali)]] are takhyilat in which feet have slipped since ancient times. Those who slipped came to grief only from their lack of care for research and investigation, so that they would know that among the ranks of the subtle sciences there is a science which, if they had measured it with its true measure, would not have remained hidden from them that all the sciences are in need of it and dependent upon it, since none can untie their knotted difficulties or unlock their hard constraints except Him. How many a verse of the revelation and how many a hadith of the Messenger have been wronged and disfigured by feeble interpretations and poor aspects, because whoever interprets without this knowledge does not know a thread of it, neither the spun yarn nor the twisted strand. [[His saying "does not know a thread of it, neither the spun yarn nor the twisted strand": in al-Sihah, "qabil" is what a woman draws from her spinning when she twists it, and "dabir" is what a woman arranges from her spinning when she twists it. From this comes the saying: so-and-so does not know a thread of it, neither the spun yarn nor the twisted strand. (Ali)]] The intended meaning of "the earth" is the seven earths, witnessed by two proofs: His saying "entirely" (jami'an) and His saying "and the heavens" (wa-al-samawat). Also, because the context is one of magnification and exaltation, it requires intensification. With the intention of collectivity and its emphasis by the word "entirely," He followed the whole with a emphasis before the predicate came, so that it would be known at the outset that the report that follows does not concern a single earth but all the earths. The "qabdah" (handful) is the single act of grasping, as in His saying ﴿So I took a handful from the trace of the Messenger﴾. The "qabdah" with a dhamma (qubdah) is the quantity grasped in the palm, and it is also said: "Give me a handful of such-and-such," meaning the sense of the handful, as a noun used for the verbal action (taswiyah bi-al-masdar), as has been narrated: [[I have not found it in this form. Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Ya'la narrated, from the transmission of Sahl from Abdullah ibn Yazid from a shaykh whom Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab met, that he heard Abu al-Darda' say: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade eating every predatory snatching and plunder, and the mujaththamah, and every animal with fangs of the beasts of prey." Abu Ya'la narrated it from the transmission of al-Ifriqi, and al-Darimi, al-Tabarani and al-Nasa'i in al-Kuna narrated it from the transmission of Abu Aws from al-Zuhri from Abu Idris from Abu Tha'laba, with the wording: "He forbade the khatfah, the mujaththamah, the nahbah, and every animal with fangs of the beasts of prey."]] that he forbade the "khatfat al-sab'" (the prey snatched by the beast), [[His saying "forbade the prey snatched by the beast": that is, the intended meaning is the thing snatched. (Ali)]] and both meanings are possible. The meaning is: the earths entirely are His handful, that is, possessed of His handful, He grasps them in one handful, meaning that the earths, despite their greatness and expanse, do not amount to more than one handful of His handfuls, as though He grasps them in one palm, just as you say: "The whole camel is the meal of Luqman, and the sip is his gulp," meaning: they are the meal of one bite and the gulp of one swallow, you mean: they do not amount to more than one unique bite of his bites and one single gulp of his gulps.

And if the meaning of "handful" is intended, it is evident, because the meaning is that the earths in their entirety are the measure which He grasps with a single palm.

If you say: What is the reasoning of the one who reads "qabdatuhu" with the accusative? I say: He made it a adverb of time, likening the indefinite to the definite. [Mutwiyyat (folded up) is from folding (al-tayy), which is the opposite of spreading out, as He said: ﴿On the day We roll up the heaven like the rolling of the scroll for writings﴾. The customary way of one who rolls up a scroll is to roll it with his right hand.] It has been said: "His handful" means His possession without any opposer or contender, and "with His right hand" means with His power. It has also been said: "Folded up in His right hand" means destroyed by His oath, because He swore that He would destroy them. Whoever smells a whiff of this knowledge of ours, let him present this interpretation to him, so that he may be entertained by wonder at it and at the one who said it, then weep out of zeal for the speech of God, which is inimitable in its eloquence, and out of what he was afflicted with of the like of such people, and what is heavier upon the spirit and more splitting to the liver: the scholars recording his words, approving of them, relating them from the pulpits, and drawing the applause of listeners toward them. It is read: "maṭwiyyāt" (folded up) according to the arrangement of the heavens in the ruling of the earth, and their entering under the handful. The accusative of "maṭwiyyāt" is a circumstantial state (hal). Glory be to Him, exalted is He above what is attributed to Him of partners. How far beyond this is His power and His greatness, and how high He is above what is associated with Him!

Q: Where does "أخرى" stand grammatically? A: It may be in the nominative or the accusative. As nominative, it is governed by His words, "then when the Trumpet is blown [once] with one blast" (fa-idha nufikha fi al-sur nafkhatun wahidatun).[[His words "as for the nominative, it is based on His words 'fa-idha nufikha'," i.e., in al-Haqqah. And his words "min qara'" mean: there. And his words "hudhifat" mean: here. (Gh.)]] As accusative, it follows the reading of one who recited nafkhatun wahidatun, and the meaning is: "And the Trumpet is blown, one blast, then it is blown in it another." It was omitted because another word indicates it and because it is known from its mention in more than one place.

It is also recited qiyaman yanzurun: they turn their eyes in all directions, like the gaze of one bewildered when a calamity has struck him. It is said: "they look to see what will be done to them." It is also permissible that qiyam means standing still and motionless in one place, because of their bewilderment.

And the earth shall shine with the light of its Lord. The Book shall be placed, the Prophets and the witnesses shall be brought, and judgment shall be passed between them with truth, and they shall not be wronged.

Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 39, verses 69–70:

God, Exalted is He, has used light as a metaphor for the truth (al-haqq), the Qur'an and the proof (al-burhan) in several places of the Revelation, and this is one of them. The meaning is: "And the earth shall shine with what He establishes in it of truth and justice, and spreads out of equity in the reckoning and the weighing of good deeds and evil deeds." It is announced that the light is a metaphor, by its being attributed to His name, because He is the Truth, the Just. The attribution of His name to the earth is because He adorns it when He spreads His justice in it, sets up the scales of His equity in it, and judges with truth among its people; and there is nothing more beautiful for lands than justice, nor more productive for them. In this attribution is also the indication that its Lord and Creator is the One who acts justly in it, whereas others than its Lord may act justly in it only by permission. Then comes what is coordinated with the shining of the earth: the placing of the Book, the bringing of the Prophets and the witnesses, and the judgment with truth, which is the light mentioned. You see people saying to a just king: "The horizons have shone with your justice, and the world has been illuminated by your equity," just as you say: "The lands have been darkened by the oppression of so-and-so." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection." [Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn Umar. Muslim has it from Jabir, and al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud from the hadith of Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As.] And just as he opened the verse by affirming justice, he closed it by negating injustice. It is also read: "wa-ushriqat" in the passive form, from "shurriqat bi-l-day'" (tushraq): when it is filled with it and made to overflow. And "ashraqahā Allah," just as you say: "He filled the earth with justice and covered it with justice."

"Al-Kitab" means the books of deeds (sahaif al-a'mal), but he dispensed with the generic name. It was also said: it is the Preserved Tablet. "Al-shuhada'" are those who bear witness for the nations and against them, from among the guardian angels and the righteous. It was also said: those who are martyred in the way of God.

In this attribution is also the indication that its Lord and Creator is the One who acts justly in it, whereas others than its Lord may act justly in it only by permission. Then comes what is coordinated with the shining of the earth: the placing of the Book, the bringing of the Prophets and the witnesses, and the judgment with truth, which is the light mentioned. You see people saying to a just king: "The horizons have shone with your justice, and the world has been illuminated by your equity," just as you say: "The lands have been darkened by the oppression of so-and-so." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection." [Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn Umar. Muslim has it from Jabir, and al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud from the hadith of Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As.] And just as he opened the verse by affirming justice, he closed it by negating injustice. It is also read: "wa-ushriqat" in the passive form, from "shurriqat bi-l-day'" (tushraq): when it is filled with it and made to overflow. And "ashraqahā Allah," just as you say: "He filled the earth with justice and covered it with justice."

"Al-Kitab" means the books of deeds (sahaif al-a'mal), but he dispensed with the generic name. It was also said: it is the Preserved Tablet. "Al-shuhada'" are those who bear witness for the nations and against them, from among the guardian angels and the righteous. It was also said: those who are martyred in the way of God.

Az-Zumar: the groups dispersed, one following another; and they have come in groups (tazammaru). He said:

"Until the ranks (zumar) of people came in succession, one group after another"

[[The words "and they have come in groups" — in another copy: tazamaru. In al-Sihah: "ihtazalat al-ibil fi al-sayr" means the camels rose up (in their march). (ʿ)]]: He said:

"Until ihtazalat zumar ba'da zumar" [[Indeed the seekers have been overwhelmed by the bounties (al-sayyub), until groups after groups rose up.]]

"Al-sayyub" originally means torrents, and it is used metaphorically (istiʿara) for abundant gifts, in the manner of a clear metaphor (tasrihiyya). "Al-ghamr" is a supporting element (tarshih), meaning that the seekers of provision have been overwhelmed by the praised one with gifts. "Ihtazalat" means they set out, proceeding from his presence; "zumar" means groups after groups.

It is also transmitted as "zumaran," in the accusative of circumstance (hal), meaning that the seekers rose up while being successive groups. According to the first reading, there is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, indicating abundance.]]

It has been said, regarding "zumar alladhina ittaqaw" (those who were conscious of God in groups), that they are the different classes: the martyrs, the ascetics, the scholars, the reciters, and others. It was also recited as "nudhur minkum" (warners from among you).

If you ask: why was "the day" added to them? I answer: they meant the meeting of this time of yours, which is the time of their entry into the Fire, not the Day of Resurrection. The use of "the day" and "the days" to refer to times of hardship is well established. They said: "Yes, indeed, messengers came to us and recited to us, but the word of God has become binding upon us: I will surely fill Hell, because of our evil deeds," just as they said: "Our misery overcame us, and we were a people who had gone astray." Thus they mentioned their deed that made the word of punishment binding, which is disbelief and misguidance.

The "al" in "al-mutakabbirin" is for the genus, because "mathwa al-mutakabbirin" is the subject (fa'il) of "bi'sa," and the fa'il of "bi'sa" is a noun defined by the definite article of the genus; or it is annexed to a similar noun, and the particular subject of dispraise is omitted, its estimated form being: "So wretched is the abode of the arrogant: Hell."

Until, when they reach it, its gates having been opened, its keepers will say, "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it, to abide therein."

Hattā (until) is the particle after which sentences are narrated, and the sentence narrated after it is the conditional clause. However, its apodosis (jawāb, the answer of the condition) is omitted. It was omitted because it describes the reward of the people of Paradise, so by omitting it he indicated that it is something no description can encompass. Its proper place is after "khālidīn" (abiding therein). It was also said: "Until when they come to it, they come to it and its gates have been opened," meaning "along with the opening of its gates."

It was also said: the gates of Hell are not opened except when its people arrive there. As for the gates of Paradise, their opening precedes their arrival, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, whose gates are opened for them﴾ [38:50]. Therefore the waw is used, as if it were said: "Until when they come to it, its gates having already been opened."

If you say: how is the going of both groups expressed by the word "driving" (sawq)? I say: what is meant by the driving of the people of the Fire is driving them toward it with humiliation and harshness, as is done to captives and to those who rebel against the ruler when they are driven to a prison or to execution. What is meant by the driving of the people of Paradise is the driving of their mounts, for they are not taken except riding, and urging them on quickly to the abode of honour and good pleasure, as is done with those of distinction and honour among the envoys to some kings. So vast is the difference between the two drivings.

﴿You are pure﴾: you are purified from the filth of sins and cleansed from the impurity of transgressions. ﴿So enter it﴾: the entry into Paradise is made dependent upon purity and cleanliness. It is nothing but the abode of the good and the dwelling place of the pure, for it is an abode that Allah has purified from every filth and cleansed from every impurity, so none enters it except one who is fitting for it and described by its attributes. How far our conditions are from that fitness, and how weak our striving is in acquiring that quality, unless the Bestower, the Generous, grants us sincere repentance that cleanses our souls from the grime of sins and removes the harm from these hearts.

﴿Abiding therein﴾: abiding eternally. ﴿The land﴾: an expression for the place in which they dwelt, took as their residence and abode. ﴿And they have inherited it﴾: that is, they have possessed it and made themselves its kings, and their disposal of it was made absolute, so they act as they wish. This is a likeness to the condition of an heir and his disposal of what he inherits, his expansiveness in it, and his spending of it lavishly, far and wide.

If you say: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿wherever we will﴾, and does one of them occupy the place of another? I say: each one of them has a garden that is indescribable in its vastness and in its abundance beyond his need, so he takes up residence in his own garden wherever he wishes, and has no need of the garden of another.

If you ask: to what does the pronoun in His words ﴿بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ refer? I say: it may refer to all the servants. Placing some in the Fire and some in the Garden is only a judgment between them with truth and justice. It may also refer to the angels, since their rewards, even though they are all protected from sin (ma'ṣūmūn), are not of one uniform degree. Rather, their ranks are distinguished according to the differences in their deeds, and that is judgment between them with truth.

If you ask: who is the speaker of His words ﴿وَقِيلَ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾? I say: those who are judged between are either all the servants or the angels. It is as if it were said: and He judged between them with truth, and they said: praise be to Allah for His judgment between us with truth, and for placing each of us in the station that is his due.

On the authority of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite Surat Banī Isrāʾīl and al-Zumar every night.
